## Introduction

### Overview

Since [week 12](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#quarto-documents),
you've been writing your R code in Quarto documents,
using a basic YAML header, code chunks, and Markdown text.
In this session, we'll take a closer look at each of these components,
and at what happens when you render a document.
We'll also see how to record the R and package versions you used,
and how to run R code and render Quarto documents in Slurm batch jobs at OSC,
which is useful for longer-running analyses.

### Learning goals

In this session, you will learn:

-   What happens when Quarto renders a document
-   More about **YAML** syntax and useful options in the YAML header
-   How to use **chunk options**, including for figures, and how to set them for a whole document
-   How to label chunks and include R output in your Markdown text
-   How to record the versions of R and R packages that you used
-   How to render a document to Markdown that displays well on GitHub
-   How to run R scripts and render Quarto documents in a Slurm batch job

## Setting up

Create a new folder `week14`,
and in it, [create a new Quarto document](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document) `week14a.qmd`.

## How rendering works

When you render a Quarto document, two programs do the work:

1. **knitr** runs all code chunks, in a new R session,
   and creates a plain Markdown file with your text, code, and the code's output.
2. **Pandoc** converts that Markdown file to the final output format.

This two-step process means that the same `.qmd` file can be rendered to many output formats,
like HTML, PDF, Word, and even slide decks and websites^[
This website and its slides were made with Quarto, too!],
and that Quarto isn't limited to R:
it can also run code in other languages like Python.
Quarto is the next-generation version of R Markdown, in case you have heard of that.

### Rendering from the terminal

You can also render a Quarto document from the terminal,
using the `quarto render` command:

```bash
quarto render week14/week14a.qmd
```

This does a **one-time render**:
just like `Preview`, it runs all code in a new R session
and creates `week14a.html` next to `week14a.qmd`.
But unlike `Preview`, it does not show the result in the Viewer pane.
To look at the output, open the HTML file yourself.

So, `Preview` is handy while you are writing and editing a document,
whereas `quarto render` is handy to simply produce the final output file.

## Components of Quarto documents

As you saw in week 12, a Quarto document has three main components:
the YAML header, code chunks, and Markdown text.
We'll take a closer look at each of these now.

### YAML header

The YAML header contains settings for the document:
metadata like the title and author,
and options for the output format.
Recall from week 12 that each line contains a `key: value` pair (with a space after the colon).
Here is an example with a few more options:

```yaml
---
title: "Week 14: Quarto"
subtitle: "Beyond the basics"
author: "Jane Doe"
date: 2026-11-23
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
---
```

- Keys can be nested by indenting them with two spaces:
  above, `html` is nested under `format`,
  and `embed-resources`, `toc`, and `theme` are options for the `html` output format.
- `embed-resources: true` makes Quarto put everything,
  including any figures, into a single HTML file,
  so you can download that one file from OSC and open or share it.
- `toc: true` adds a table of contents.
- `theme` picks one of Quarto's
  [25 built-in themes](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html),
  which change the fonts, colors, etc.
- There are many more [options for HTML output](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html).

::: callout-tip
#### Project-level YAML
You can also set YAML options for all Quarto documents in a project
in a file called `_quarto.yml` in the project's root directory
(see the [Quarto docs on projects](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/project-configuration.html)).
Options in a document's own YAML header override these.
:::

#### Quotes

In YAML, strings usually don't need quotes,
but they do when they contain special characters like `:` or `#`.
For example, the title in the example above, `"Week 14: Quarto"`, needs quotes because of the colon.
To be safe, you can always quote strings.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More YAML syntax: lists and comments _(Click to expand)_
Some keys take a list of values, which can be written in two ways:

```yaml
# Block syntax: each item on a new line, preceded by a dash and a space
author:
  - Jane Doe
  - John Smith

# Inline syntax: comma-separated values inside square brackets
keywords: [RNA-seq, mosquito, Plasmodium]
```

As in R and the shell, a `#` starts a comment.
:::

### Code chunks

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Showing the output below each chunk _(Click to expand)_
Positron can optionally show the output of each chunk right below it in the editor,
as RStudio does by default.
To turn this on, open the Settings and enable `quarto.inlineOutput.enabled`.

With this setting turned on,
Positron runs the code of each Quarto document in a separate R session,
whose working directory is the document's folder,
and whose Console is not shown by default
(to show it, enable `console.showNotebookConsoles`).
Because you use `here()` for file paths
([week 13](../week13/w13a_data-wrangling.qmd#file-paths-in-quarto-documents)),
your code works the same either way.
:::

#### Chunk options

You can change how a chunk behaves with **chunk options**:
lines at the top of a chunk that start with `#|`,
where each `#|` line sets one option.
For example, this chunk would be shown in the rendered document, but not run:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

A few useful chunk options:

- `#| eval: false` --- Show the code but don't run it.
- `#| echo: false` --- Run the code and show its output, but hide the code itself.
  This is useful if you want to show a figure but not the code used to create it.
- `#| include: false` --- Run the code, but show neither the code nor its output.
- `#| warning: false` and `#| message: false` --- Hide warnings and messages,
  such as the ones printed when loading some packages.
- `#| fig-show: hide` --- Hide figures.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Install packages in the console rather than in a chunk.
Otherwise, they will be installed again every time you render the document.
:::

Chunk options can also be written inside the curly braces,
as in ```` ```{r, echo=FALSE} ````,
but the `#|` syntax is preferred.
More chunk options can be found
[here](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html).

#### Figure options

When you render a document, any plots made in code chunks are included in the output.
Several chunk options control how plots are shown --- for example:

```{r}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| fig-cap: "Body mass of penguins on different islands"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

- `fig-cap` --- Add a figure caption below the plot.
- `fig-width` and `fig-height` --- Set the size of the plot (in inches).
- `fig-align` --- Align the plot to the `left`, `right`, or `center`.

#### Global vs. chunk-specific options

If the default code chunk settings don’t fit your needs, you can change
them for the whole document in the YAML section under `execute:`. For
example, if you don’t want to show your R code to your readers, you can
set `echo: false` which hides all code by default. If you later want to
show the code for a specific chunk, you can turn it back on just for
that chunk using `echo: true`.
For example:

```yaml
---
title: "My report"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---
```

Note that `execute:` is a top-level key, not nested under `format:`.

#### Chunk labels

You can give a chunk a **label** with `#| label: <label-name>`.
Labels must be unique within a document and cannot contain spaces.
They show up in messages during rendering,
which makes it easier to find the chunk that caused a problem:

```{r}
#| label: my-first-chunk
#| echo: fenced
2 + 3
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Besides `Run Cell`, which runs the current chunk,
the line above each chunk has a `Run Above` button,
which runs all code chunks _above_ the current chunk.
This is useful when you've restarted R or opened a document in a new session,
and want to get back to where you were.
:::

### Markdown text

The "default text" in Quarto documents is Markdown, unlike in R scripts,
where everything is considered code until commented out by `#`.
Quarto text syntax is based on Pandoc Markdown which is similar to
the original Markdown syntax we discussed in
[week 2](../week02/w2d_markdown.qmd).

#### Inline code

You can include the output of R code directly in your Markdown text with **inline code**:
a backtick, the letter `r` and a space, your code, and a closing backtick.
For example, this text:

```markdown
The iris data set contains `r "\x60r nrow(iris)\x60"` flowers.
```

Renders as:

> The iris data set contains `r nrow(iris)` flowers.

This way, numbers in your text are computed when you render the document,
so they always match your data and code --- no more copy-pasting numbers.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: Inline code

1. Add a sentence to your document that reports the number of rows of the `diamonds`
   data set with inline code, and render.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For example: The diamonds data set has `r "\x60r nrow(diamonds)\x60"` rows.

   </details>

2. **Predict**: what will the rendered document show if you leave out the `r` and the space,
   i.e. `` `nrow(diamonds)` ``? Render to check.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Without the `r`, it is regular Markdown inline code formatting:
   the text `nrow(diamonds)` is shown in a code font, and the code is not run.

   </details>
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The visual editor _(Click to expand)_

So far, you've edited Quarto documents in the default **source editor**,
where you type everything yourself:
the text, the code chunks, and the YAML header.
This gives you full control, but requires knowing some Markdown and Quarto syntax.

Positron also has a **visual editor** for Quarto documents,
which is the same one you may have used for Markdown files in VS Code in
[week 7](../week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#markdown-setup),
since both use the Quarto extension.
In the visual editor, you can format text and add elements like tables and images
with toolbar buttons, and see roughly how your document will look as you write,
much like in Word or Google Docs.

To switch between the two editors,
click the `...` button in the top-right of the editor,
and select "**Edit in Visual Mode**" or "**Edit in Source Mode**".

<!---- TODO: Add a Positron screenshot of a Quarto document in the visual editor ---->
:::

## Recording R and package versions

For reproducibility, it's good practice to record which versions of R and R packages you used.
An easy way to do so is to end each Quarto document with a chunk that runs `sessionInfo()`.
Its output lists your R version, your operating system,
and the versions of all loaded packages:

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```

`sessionInfo()` only _records_ package versions.
To also be able to _restore_ them,
you can give each project its own package library with **renv** ---
see the [optional self-study page on renv](../bonus/renv.qmd).

## Output for GitHub

GitHub shows HTML files as raw code, not as web pages.
To share a rendered document in a GitHub repository, like for your final project,
you can _also_ render it to GitHub-Flavored Markdown (`gfm`), which GitHub displays nicely:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
  gfm: default
```

With two formats, the `Preview` button only renders the first one.
To render both formats,
use `quarto render` in the terminal, as shown [above](#rendering-from-the-terminal).
This creates a `.md` file, plus a `_files` folder with the figures:
commit both to your repository.

## Running R in a Slurm batch job

So far, you've run all your R code interactively, in Positron.
But some analyses take a long time to run,
like differential expression analyses of large data sets,
or simply rendering a document whose code takes an hour.
Instead of keeping Positron open (your compute job ends after a few hours),
you can run such code in a **Slurm batch job**, like you did with shell scripts in
[week 10](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd).

There are two commands to run R code from the shell:

- `Rscript my-script.R` runs an R script (`.R` file) from start to finish
  (see the box on R scripts in
  [week 12](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#rendering)).
- `quarto render my-doc.qmd` renders a Quarto document,
  like you did in the terminal [above](#rendering-from-the-terminal).

Here is a shell script that renders a Quarto document in a batch job:

<!----
TODO: Test at OSC whether `quarto` is available in a batch job.
Positron bundles Quarto, and batch jobs inherit the environment of the shell they're submitted from,
so it should work when submitted from Positron's terminal: check `which quarto` there, and submit the script once.
If it doesn't work, use the full path to Positron's bundled `quarto` in the script.
---->

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/render.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS3493
#SBATCH --time=60
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL
#SBATCH --output=slurm-render-%j.out

# Load R (this is the same module as in your ~/.bashrc)
module load gcc/12.3.0 R/4.6.1

set -euo pipefail

# Copy the placeholder variables
qmd_file=$1

# Render the Quarto document
quarto render "$qmd_file"
```

<!----
TODO: Check whether `module load` actually fails after `set -euo pipefail` at OSC
(a known Lmod issue in some setups, not confirmed at OSC).
If it works fine, remove the second bullet point below and use the usual order.
---->

- Unlike most software in this course, we load R with an OSC module rather than a container,
  because that's the R installation that you installed all your packages for.
- The `module load` line comes before `set -euo pipefail`,
  because the `module` command can fail with the strict settings of `set -u`.
- To run an R script instead, replace `quarto render` with `Rscript`,
  and pass the script an R script instead of a Quarto document.

You would submit this script as follows:

```bash
sbatch scripts/render.sh week14/week14a.qmd
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Render a document in a batch job

1. Create the script above as `scripts/render.sh` in your personal dir,
   and submit it to render your `week14a.qmd`.

2. When the job has finished, check the Slurm log file and the rendered HTML file.
   Was the HTML file updated? (Hint: `ls -l` shows when a file was last modified.)

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   The Slurm log file `slurm-render-<job-id>.out` should contain the same
   rendering messages you see when you render in the terminal,
   and `ls -l week14` should show that `week14a.html` was just modified.

   </details>
---->
:::

## Before next week: install packages for week 15

Installing the R packages for next week's RNA-seq analysis takes a few minutes,
so let's get that started now.
Run the following code in the R console ---
we'll go over what these commands do next week:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("BiocManager")
install.packages("pheatmap")
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")
```

If the installation doesn't finish before the end of class,
or you weren't able to start it,
please make sure to run it before next week's class
(see the [week 15 overview](../week15/w15_overview.qmd#before-class-install-packages)).
